source: A satellite alert system launched in 2021 has helped rangers in the Tamar Forest reduce illegal logging by 43 percent, according to the environment ministry. The system compares radar images every six days, which can see through clouds, and sends a message to patrol teams when it detects that trees have been cleared in an area larger than 0.1 hectare. Before the system, rangers often discovered clearings weeks later, when the timber had already been removed. Today, teams reach 70 percent of alerts within 72 hours and have confiscated 1,300 cubic meters of illegally cut wood. The program costs 1.8 million dollars per year, and it has been funded by a grant from a European development agency. Local communities are being trained to verify alerts using smartphones, which also gives them a role in protecting the forest.
target_summary: Satellite alerts cut illegal logging in Tamar Forest by 43 percent.

source: The Harrowdown stone circle, built about 4,500 years ago on a windswept moor, consists of 27 standing stones arranged in a ring 38 meters wide. A survey published this year found that the entrance gap lines up with the point on the horizon where the sun rises on the midsummer solstice, and that two tall stones on the opposite side frame the midwinter sunset. Archaeologist Fiona Garrick said that the builders must have observed the sky for generations to place the stones with such accuracy, since errors are less than one degree. Excavations also uncovered burned bone and pottery fragments, suggesting that the site was used for gatherings and ceremonies, perhaps at the turning points of the agricultural year. The circle is open to the public, and about 15,000 people visit every year.
target_summary: Harrowdown stone circle aligns with solstice sunrise and sunset.

source: Hospitals often serve unappetizing meals that patients leave half-eaten, which contributes to malnutrition and slower recovery. In response, the Kingsmead General Hospital introduced a room-service system in 2022, allowing patients to order meals from a menu by phone at any time between 7 a.m. and 7 p.m. and have them delivered within 45 minutes. Chefs prepare dishes to order, and dietitians check choices for patients with special needs. A review found that patients ate 30 percent more of their food, that food waste fell from 41 to 18 percent, and that the average length of stay shortened by half a day. Food costs fell by 9 percent because less was thrown away, which offset the extra cost of staff. Patient satisfaction scores for meals rose from 54 to 86 percent.
target_summary: Kingsmead hospital's room-service meals raised eating and cut food waste.

source: Consumers lose billions of dollars each year to subscriptions that they forget to cancel, and new rules aim to make leaving as easy as joining. Under regulations taking effect in September, companies that allow customers to sign up online must offer a cancellation option that takes no more steps than signing up, and they must send a reminder before any free trial turns into a paid plan. A survey of 2,000 adults found that the average household pays for 4.3 subscriptions that it rarely uses, costing about 340 dollars annually. Businesses have objected that the rules will raise costs and cut conversions, though some have already simplified the process. Violations can be punished with fines of up to 10,000 dollars per case. Consumer advocates advise people to review their bank statements every three months.
target_summary: New rules require subscription cancellation to be as easy as signing up.

source: A study of 60 recreational runners found that listening to music with a tempo matched to their running pace, about 160 to 170 beats per minute, increased the distance they covered in 30 minutes by an average of 4 percent compared with running without music. Participants also rated the effort as easier, even though their heart rates were the same. Researchers explain the effect through synchronization: runners unconsciously match their steps to the beat, which makes their movement more efficient, and music also distracts from the sensation of fatigue. The benefits were smaller for experienced runners, who tend to focus on their own body signals, and the effect disappeared when the music was very slow. The authors advise runners who train in busy places to keep volume low enough to hear traffic.
target_summary: Running to music matched to pace increased distance by 4 percent.

source: Shipping lines have discovered that slowing down saves a great deal of fuel, since the energy required to move a ship increases sharply with speed. By reducing the cruising speed of container ships from 24 knots to 18, a practice known as slow steaming, operators can cut fuel consumption by about 40 percent on a given voyage. The approach adds days to journeys: a crossing from Shanghai to Rotterdam takes about 6 days longer, which requires more ships to keep the same weekly schedule. Because fuel accounts for roughly half of a ship's operating costs, most large carriers have adopted the practice, and it has reduced the industry's carbon emissions per container. Recent regulations that limit the carbon intensity of ships have encouraged even slower speeds, although retailers complain of delays for goods that are needed urgently.
target_summary: Slow steaming cuts container ships' fuel use about 40 percent.

source: A trial in 24 primary schools in the district of Bellwood found that children who spent one hour a week in a school garden scored 12 percent higher on science tests than children who learned the same material entirely in classrooms. The pupils, aged 8 to 11, planted vegetables, measured plant growth, and kept records, which linked lessons on biology and math to hands-on tasks. Teachers also reported that children were more willing to try vegetables, and in surveys 61 percent of the garden group said they ate more vegetables at home. Each garden cost about 1,800 dollars to build, and schools relied on parent volunteers for upkeep during vacations. A few schools struggled with a lack of space or with vandalism, and the district is considering raised beds on rooftops for crowded city schools.
target_summary: School gardens raised science scores 12 percent in a 24-school trial.

source: Farmers in the dry district of Rawat have adopted drip irrigation on 14,000 hectares in five years, after a subsidy program covered 60 percent of the cost of the equipment. Drip systems deliver water through small pipes directly to the roots of each plant, cutting water use by about 40 percent compared with flooding fields, and they allow fertilizer to be applied precisely. A study of 300 farms found that cotton yields rose 22 percent and farmers' incomes grew by 31 percent, mostly because of higher yields and lower labor costs. However, smaller farmers had trouble paying the remaining 40 percent of the cost, and pipes clogged when water was not filtered properly. The district is introducing low-interest loans and training sessions on maintenance, and it expects drip irrigation to cover half of the farmland by 2030.
target_summary: Drip irrigation raised cotton yields and incomes in Rawat district.

source: The price of a concert ticket shows how supply and demand work. When a band announces a show in a hall that holds 5,000 people, and 20,000 fans want to buy tickets at the original price of 80 dollars, demand exceeds supply. If prices were allowed to rise freely, they might climb to 250 dollars before demand fell to match the number of seats. Resale websites let this happen, and the result is that the tickets go to those who value them most, or at least those who can pay most. Organizers who keep prices low must use another way to ration seats, such as lotteries or queues. Economists note that the supply of seats is fixed in the short term, so higher prices cannot create more of them, though they might encourage additional shows.
target_summary: Concert ticket prices illustrate supply and demand when demand exceeds supply.

source: A microwave oven heats food by sending electromagnetic waves, at a frequency of 2.45 gigahertz, into the cooking chamber. Water molecules in the food are electrically uneven, with a slightly positive end and a slightly negative end, so they rotate back and forth billions of times per second as the waves alternate. This rapid movement causes friction between molecules, which produces heat. Microwaves penetrate only about one to two centimeters into most foods, so the outer layers heat first and the middle warms by conduction, which is why stirring and standing time help even out temperatures. The metal walls of the oven reflect the waves, keeping them inside, and a rotating plate moves food through hot and cold spots. Metal objects such as foil can cause sparks, since the waves induce electric currents in them.
target_summary: Microwaves heat food by rotating water molecules, producing friction heat.

source: The Eastgate Public Library now lends more than books: its Library of Things allows members to borrow 1,400 items, including power drills, sewing machines, camping tents, and telescopes, for up to three weeks. The program began in 2022 with 200 items, funded by a 45,000 dollar grant, and has recorded 11,500 loans, with drills and pressure washers among the most popular. Library staff say that it helps residents save money on equipment they only need occasionally, and reduces clutter and waste. Items are checked by volunteers after each loan, and about 3 percent have been damaged or lost, a figure lower than expected. Borrowers must attend a short safety demonstration before taking out power tools. The library plans to add musical instruments and kitchen equipment next year, funded by donations.
target_summary: Eastgate library lends 1,400 tools and household items.

source: Eight years after hosting the Summer Games, the city of Varnholt has turned its Olympic stadium into a home for a professional football club, and the athletes' village into 3,400 apartments. Planners had learned from other cities where venues stood empty, and they designed the 60,000-seat stadium so that its upper tiers could be removed after the Games, reducing capacity to 35,000. The swimming pool is now used by 2,000 children and clubs each week, and the cycling track hosts national championships. Not everything has gone smoothly: the cost of maintaining the arena is 4.2 million dollars per year, which is covered only partly by rent, and a planned tennis center was cancelled for lack of funding. The city says the regeneration of the surrounding district has attracted 7,500 new jobs.
target_summary: Varnholt reused its Olympic stadium and athletes' village after the Games.

source: When wolves were reintroduced to Aspen Valley National Park in 1996 after seventy years of absence, scientists noticed changes that went far beyond the wolves themselves. The elk population, which had grown unchecked, dropped from 19,000 to about 8,000 as wolves hunted them, and the elk also changed their behavior, avoiding open river valleys where they could be ambushed. As a result, willows and aspens recovered along the streams, which provided habitat for beavers and songbirds, and the shade cooled the water for trout. Researchers call this effect a trophic cascade, in which predators influence the lower levels of the food web. The extent of the cascade is still debated, since weather and other predators also influenced vegetation, but studies agree that the return of wolves has changed the ecosystem.
target_summary: Wolf reintroduction reduced elk and revived streamside vegetation in Aspen Valley.

source: A survey of 1,500 independent app developers found that 62 percent consider the 30 percent fee charged by the major app stores on in-app purchases to be a significant barrier to profitability. target_summary: Most surveyed app developers say 30 percent store fees hurt profitability.

source: Sales of plant-based meat products in the country fell 12 percent last year, to 1.1 billion dollars, after several years of rapid growth, according to a market research firm. Surveys found that many people tried the products once but did not buy them again, citing price, which averages about 35 percent more than ordinary meat, and taste. Health concerns have also played a role, since some consumers dislike the long list of ingredients and the high salt content. Manufacturers are responding by cutting prices, simplifying recipes, and launching new products, such as chicken-style nuggets that have performed better than burgers. Industry observers say that a decline after an initial burst is normal for new food categories, and they note that sales of plant-based milk, which now accounts for 15 percent of milk sales, show that substitutes can succeed.
target_summary: Plant-based meat sales fell 12 percent after repeat purchases declined.

source: A study of 12,000 adults over 65 found that a wristband sensor can detect atrial fibrillation, an irregular heartbeat that raises the risk of stroke, with a sensitivity of 87 percent. Participants wore the device for two weeks, and those whose readings suggested an irregular rhythm were referred for confirmation with a standard electrocardiogram. Of the 410 people who received alerts, 62 percent were confirmed to have the condition, and most had not known about it. They were then offered treatment with blood thinners, which reduce the risk of stroke by about two thirds. The researchers note that false alarms can cause anxiety and unnecessary appointments, and that the benefits of widespread screening of people with no symptoms are not proven. A larger trial of 50,000 participants will measure whether screening actually prevents strokes.
target_summary: A wristband detected atrial fibrillation with 87 percent sensitivity in seniors.

source: In the weeks before the Carnival of Santa Marta, the workshops of the city's costume makers are working day and night. About 4,500 people, many of them women working from home, sew sequins, feathers, and beads onto costumes for the 90 dance groups that parade through the streets. An elaborate costume can take 300 hours to make and sells for between 400 and 2,000 dollars, while the largest ones, worn by lead dancers, can weigh up to 25 kilograms. The industry generates an estimated 38 million dollars annually and supports families throughout the year, since groups order outfits months ahead. Rising prices for imported materials have squeezed profits, and makers worry that cheaper factory products will undercut them. The city has launched a training program to teach young people the craft and a label to certify handmade costumes.
target_summary: Santa Marta's carnival costume industry employs 4,500 people.

source: The Westfield Power Station, a coal plant that supplied electricity to 600,000 homes for 52 years, closed in 2022, and its site is being converted into a 420-megawatt solar farm with a battery storage facility. The project reuses the existing grid connection, which saves about 30 million dollars and years of waiting for permits, and it occupies 700 hectares, including former ash ponds that were capped and cleaned. Developers say that the solar farm will generate about 800 gigawatt-hours of power per year, about 60 percent of what the old plant produced. The conversion will employ 250 people during construction, but only 25 permanently, compared with 400 at the coal plant. To help workers, the company has offered retraining and funded a 5 million dollar community fund for the surrounding town.
target_summary: Westfield's closed coal plant site will become a 420-megawatt solar farm.

source: The first transatlantic telegraph cable was completed on 5 August 1858, connecting Newfoundland and Ireland and cutting the time for a message to cross the ocean from about ten days by ship to a few minutes. Queen Victoria and President Buchanan exchanged greetings over the line, and celebrations were held in New York. However, the cable was poorly insulated, and operators struggled to send messages: the queen's greeting of 98 words took 16 hours to transmit. After a high voltage was applied in an attempt to speed it up, the insulation failed and the cable went dead after only three weeks. A more reliable cable was successfully laid in 1866 using the large steamship Great Eastern, and it began a lasting link between the two continents.
target_summary: The 1858 transatlantic telegraph cable worked briefly before failing.

source: Legal aid clinics provide free or low-cost legal advice to people who cannot afford lawyers, often on issues such as housing, family disputes, and benefits. The Southside Legal Clinic, staffed by 14 lawyers and 90 volunteers, helped 6,200 people last year, and about half of its cases involved tenants facing eviction. A study found that tenants represented by the clinic stayed in their homes in 68 percent of cases, compared with 29 percent of those who had no lawyer. Demand far exceeds capacity, though, and the clinic turns away about 3,000 people each year because it lacks funding. Government grants have fallen by 20 percent in a decade, and the clinic relies on donations and law firms that provide free work. Its director has asked the city council for 1.5 million dollars to hire eight more lawyers.
target_summary: Southside Legal Clinic helps tenants stay housed but turns away thousands.

source: After a public campaign by nutrition groups, six of the country's largest breakfast cereal producers agreed to cut the sugar content of their children's cereals by 20 percent over three years. A typical bowl of sweetened cereal contained 12 grams of sugar, about three teaspoons, which is half of the daily limit recommended for young children. By the end of the second year, the average sugar content had fallen to 9.8 grams per serving, and the companies reported little change in sales, partly because they reduced sugar gradually so that consumers did not notice the difference. Health experts welcomed the progress but said that voluntary agreements have limits, since some brands had not signed up. They also noted that many cereals remain high in sugar and called for clearer front-of-pack labels.
target_summary: Cereal makers agreed to cut children's cereal sugar 20 percent over three years.

source: Ocean acidification, which happens when seawater absorbs carbon dioxide from the air, has made it difficult for baby oysters to form their shells. Since 2007, oyster hatcheries on the northwest coast have suffered several mass die-offs of larvae, in one year losing 80 percent of their production. Shell formation requires carbonate, which becomes scarcer as water becomes more acidic. Hatchery operators have responded by monitoring the chemistry of the water continuously and adding sodium carbonate to the tanks to raise its pH when needed, and some now draw water only in the afternoon, when algae have removed some carbon dioxide. These measures restored larval survival to about 70 percent. Scientists are also breeding oysters that are more tolerant of acid conditions, but they warn that these solutions cannot protect wild oysters.
target_summary: Ocean acidification hampers baby oysters' shells, forcing hatcheries to adapt.

source: The airline industry expects to need 650,000 new pilots worldwide over the next 20 years, but training a commercial pilot costs 80,000 to 120,000 dollars and takes up to two years, which deters many applicants. To widen the pipeline, Regional Wings Airlines has launched a cadet program in which it pays 70 percent of training costs in exchange for a six-year employment commitment. The first group of 120 cadets began flight school in September, and about one third of them are women, compared with 5 percent of the airline's current pilots. Instructors say that many young people did not consider flying because of the cost. Union representatives welcomed the initiative but warned that cadets who leave early may be required to pay back large sums, and they have asked the company to limit the repayment to the amount actually spent.
target_summary: Regional Wings will fund 70 percent of pilot training for cadets.

source: A tonne of old mobile phones contains about 300 grams of gold, which is roughly 30 to 50 times more than a tonne of gold ore, yet only 17 percent of the world's electronic waste is formally recycled. The rest is buried, burned, or processed informally in poor conditions, releasing toxic metals such as lead and mercury. A recycling plant in the city of Norvik now recovers gold, silver, copper, and palladium from circuit boards by shredding them, melting the metal fractions, and refining them using electricity instead of chemicals. The facility processes 30,000 tonnes of electronics per year and says that producing copper from scrap uses about 85 percent less energy than mining it. The company has asked the government for rules requiring manufacturers to fund collection of old devices, which could raise recycling rates.
target_summary: Electronics recycling recovers gold and copper efficiently, but few devices are recycled.

source: The Mojave Reach Energy Storage Facility, which began operating in March, is the largest battery installation in the country, able to deliver 400 megawatts for four hours, enough to supply about 300,000 homes during the evening peak. The 560 million dollar system consists of 1,500 shipping-container-sized units of lithium iron phosphate batteries and charges when solar power is abundant at midday, then releases electricity after sunset, when demand is highest and prices are three times as high. Grid operators say it replaced a gas-fired peaker plant that had run for only 300 hours per year. During a heat wave in July, the facility discharged at full power for four hours and helped avoid blackouts. Fire safety was a major community concern, and the plant includes gas detection, automatic ventilation, and spacing between units.
target_summary: Mojave Reach's 400-megawatt battery stores solar power for evening peaks.

source: The University of Fenmore has cut its first-year dropout rate from 17 percent to 11 percent since introducing an early-warning system that identifies struggling students within the first six weeks. The software combines data on class attendance, use of the online learning platform, and grades on early assignments, and it flags students who show a pattern linked to leaving. Advisers then contact the student by phone or text, and they offer tutoring, financial counseling, or help with housing, depending on the problem. A review of 5,200 students found that those who received outreach were 34 percent more likely to remain enrolled than similar students who were flagged but contacted late. Privacy advocates asked for clear rules about how the data is used, and the university has promised that the information will be used only to provide support, not for grading.
target_summary: Fenmore's early-warning system cut first-year dropout from 17 to 11 percent.

The software combines data on class attendance, use of the online learning platform, and grades on early assignments, and it flags students who show a pattern linked to leaving. Advisers then contact the student by phone or text, and they offer tutoring, financial counseling, or help with housing, depending on the problem. A review of 5,200 students found that those who received outreach were 34 percent more likely to remain enrolled than similar students who were flagged but contacted late. Privacy advocates asked for clear rules about how the data is used, and the university has promised that the information will be used only to provide support, not for grading.
target_summary: Fenmore University's early-warning software uses attendance, platform use, and early grades to flag struggling students for tutoring or financial help, cutting first-year dropout from 17 to 11 percent; privacy advocates want clear data rules.

source: Green roofs, which are covered in soil and plants, can cut the temperature of a building's surface by as much as 30 degrees Celsius on a hot day, and they also absorb rainwater and provide habitat for insects and birds. A city-wide program in Ostwick has installed them on 260 public and commercial buildings since 2016, covering 31 hectares, and offers building owners a subsidy of 40 dollars per square meter. Measurements show that the roofs retain about 60 percent of the rain that falls on them, which reduces pressure on storm drains, and that top-floor rooms stay about 3 degrees cooler in summer. Installing a green roof costs two to three times as much as a conventional one, and it requires extra structural support, but the roofs can last twice as long because the plants protect the waterproof layer.
target_summary: Ostwick's green roofs cool buildings and absorb rainwater.

source: The World Health Organization estimates that more than one billion young people are at risk of hearing loss from listening to loud music through headphones and at concerts. Sound is measured in decibels, and prolonged exposure to levels above 85 decibels, roughly that of heavy city traffic, can damage the tiny hair cells in the inner ear, which do not grow back. Earbuds at maximum volume can produce more than 100 decibels, which can cause harm in as little as 15 minutes. Audiologists suggest following the 60-60 rule: listen at no more than 60 percent of maximum volume for no more than 60 minutes at a time. Noise-canceling headphones help, since people turn up the volume less when background noise is blocked. Early signs of damage include ringing in the ears and difficulty following conversations in noisy rooms.
target_summary: Loud headphones risk hearing loss; follow the 60-60 rule.

source: A retirement community in the town of Ostveld allows six university students to live rent-free in small apartments within the complex, provided that they spend at least 30 hours per month with the residents. The students, who have included engineering and nursing majors, help with shopping, share meals, and teach older neighbors how to use tablets and video calls. Residents say that the young people bring energy and conversation, and staff report that residents who take part are less lonely and more physically active. The experiment started in 2012 and has since inspired programs in more than 20 cities. Costs are low, since the apartments were previously empty, but organizers say that selecting the right students is essential: applicants undergo interviews, and about one in four is accepted.
target_summary: Ostveld students live rent-free with retirees in exchange for companionship.

source: The Metrolink transit agency has introduced contactless payment on all its trains and buses, allowing passengers to tap a bank card or phone instead of buying a ticket. Fares are automatically capped, so a rider who makes several trips in a day never pays more than the price of a day pass, which is 7.50 dollars, and weekly spending is capped at 31 dollars. In the first six months, 58 percent of trips were paid for by contactless methods, and queues at ticket machines dropped by about half. The agency saves money because it can retire 400 aging ticket machines and reduce cash handling. Some passengers without bank accounts or smartphones have been left out, so the agency has kept prepaid cards that can be purchased with cash at 1,200 shops and will maintain them for at least five years.
target_summary: Metrolink introduced contactless fare payment with daily and weekly caps.

source: Heirloom seed libraries let gardeners borrow seeds in spring, grow the plants, and return seeds from the best specimens in autumn, preserving varieties that are no longer sold commercially. The Fairhaven Seed Library, which operates from a corner of the public library, holds 640 varieties of vegetables, herbs, and flowers, including a purple bean that was grown in the region in the 1800s and a tomato variety donated by a 91-year-old farmer. In its first year, 1,100 members took out 9,000 seed packets, and about a third of them returned seeds. Volunteers test the seeds for germination each winter and teach classes on seed saving. Seed libraries help protect genetic diversity, since modern agriculture relies on only about 12 plants and five animal species for 75 percent of the world's food.
target_summary: Fairhaven Seed Library preserves heirloom varieties by lending seeds.

source: Fjords are long, narrow inlets of the sea surrounded by steep cliffs, and they are formed by glaciers. During ice ages, huge glaciers flowed through river valleys toward the coast, carving them into deep U-shaped troughs by grinding rock with the boulders embedded in the ice. When the climate warmed and the ice melted, the sea level rose and flooded the valleys. Fjords can be remarkably deep: Norway's Sognefjord reaches 1,308 meters, and it stretches 205 kilometers inland. Many have a shallow ridge, called a sill, near their mouth, which is the remains of the glacier's end point and limits the exchange of water with the open sea. Fjords occur in places that were glaciated, such as Norway, Chile, New Zealand, Greenland, and Canada's western coast, and they are popular with tourists.
target_summary: Glaciers carve fjords, which the sea floods after ice melts.

source: Scientists can now find out which fish live in a river by testing a liter of its water. Animals constantly shed DNA in the form of skin cells, mucus, and waste, and this environmental DNA, or eDNA, can be filtered from water and compared against reference libraries. In a survey of the Orrin River, a team from the University of Delmar collected 40 water samples and identified 52 fish species, including 6 that traditional netting had missed in the previous five years. The method is cheaper than netting, costing about 60 dollars per site, and it does not harm the animals. It also has limitations: it cannot show how many fish are present or how old they are, and DNA can drift downstream, so a positive result does not always show exactly where the animal lived.
target_summary: Environmental DNA in river water can identify fish species.

source: The Civic Museum of Natural History began offering free admission on the first Sunday of each month in 2022, and visits on those days now average 4,800 people, compared with 1,100 on a typical paid Sunday. A survey of free-day visitors found that 46 percent had never visited the museum before, and that 38 percent lived in neighborhoods with household incomes below the city median. The museum lost about 62,000 dollars in ticket revenue per year, but it recovered about half through additional sales in the cafe and shop, and donations increased by 14 percent. Staff say that the crowds can be overwhelming, with queues of up to an hour, and the museum is considering timed tickets for free days. Trustees are discussing whether to extend free entry to all children under 16.
target_summary: Free first Sundays quadrupled Civic Museum visits and attracted newcomers.

source: The modern bicycle developed gradually during the nineteenth century. In 1817, the German baron Karl von Drais built a wooden two-wheeled machine that riders pushed along with their feet, known as the running machine. Pedals were added to the front wheel in the 1860s in France, but the resulting velocipede was heavy and uncomfortable, earning the nickname boneshaker. The next step was the penny-farthing, with an enormous front wheel that allowed greater speed but was dangerous, since riders fell from a great height. The breakthrough came in 1885, when John Kemp Starley introduced the safety bicycle, which had two wheels of equal size and a chain driving the rear wheel. Pneumatic tires, invented by John Dunlop in 1888, made riding smoother, and bicycles soon became popular with women and workers.
target_summary: The bicycle evolved from the 1817 running machine to the 1885 safety bicycle.

source: The furniture maker Alder and Oak, based in a former warehouse in Bristol, builds tables and shelving from timber salvaged from demolished buildings, old barns, and shipping pallets. Each year the company reclaims about 90 tonnes of wood, which would otherwise be burned or sent to landfills, and sells it as finished furniture at prices 20 to 30 percent above those of comparable new items. Founder Marcus Webb said that customers value the character of old wood, including nail holes and weathered surfaces, as well as its history. The business employs 14 people and has annual sales of 2.2 million dollars. Challenges include removing metal fragments, which can damage tools, and securing a steady supply, since demolition schedules are unpredictable. Webb plans to open a second workshop next year, and to train apprentices in traditional joinery.

source: Colds and influenza are both respiratory infections caused by viruses, but flu is usually more severe. A cold starts gradually with a sore throat, a runny nose, and sneezing, and most people feel better within a week. Flu, by contrast, often begins suddenly with a high fever, body aches, headache, and extreme tiredness, and it can last for two weeks or longer. Flu can also lead to serious complications such as pneumonia, especially in people over 65, young children, pregnant women, and people with chronic illnesses. Antibiotics do not work against either illness, because they target bacteria, but antiviral drugs can shorten the length of flu if taken within 48 hours of the first symptoms. A yearly vaccine reduces the risk of catching flu by about 40 to 60 percent when it matches the circulating strains.
target_summary: Flu is more severe than colds; antibiotics treat neither.

source: After the city of Torsberg closed a 700-meter section of its main shopping street to cars in 2021, many shop owners feared that business would collapse. Instead, a study by the city's economic office found that foot traffic rose by 32 percent and that retail sales on the street grew by 9 percent in the first two years, while sales in comparable streets elsewhere in the city were flat. Cafes and restaurants gained most, since they were able to place tables on the former roadway. Surveys showed that shoppers who arrived by foot, bicycle, or tram spent less per visit than drivers but came more often, so their total spending was higher. Delivery vehicles are permitted before 10 a.m., and a nearby parking garage added 200 spaces. The city plans to pedestrianize two more streets.
target_summary: Closing Torsberg's main street to cars increased foot traffic and sales.

source: The Northern Moor Dark Sky Reserve, covering 1,100 square kilometers of uplands, was designated in 2020 for the quality of its night skies, where the Milky Way is clearly visible on moonless nights. To qualify, the 14 villages inside the reserve replaced about 3,000 street lamps with shielded, warm-toned lights that point downward and switch off after midnight, and they asked residents to adopt similar lighting. Astro-tourism has grown from a small niche into an industry worth about 6 million dollars a year, with hotels hosting stargazing events and offering telescopes to guests. source: More than 200 universities in the country now offer scholarships to students who play competitive video games, and the amount of money awarded has risen from 1 million dollars in 2016 to an estimated 15 million dollars this year. Teams practice for 15 to 20 hours per week with coaches, review recordings of their matches, and compete in leagues against other colleges. Supporters say that the programs attract students who might not otherwise attend college, and that they teach teamwork, communication, and strategy. Critics argue that the scholarships are small, typically between 1,000 and 5,000 dollars, and that gaming can encourage unhealthy habits, so several universities require students to attend workshops on exercise, sleep, and screen time. A few schools have begun linking the teams to degree programs in computer science and sports management.
target_summary: Over 200 universities now offer esports scholarships.

source: The Colosseum in Rome, officially called the Flavian Amphitheatre, was completed in 80 CE under the emperor Titus. The oval stadium, built of travertine limestone, tuff, and brick-faced concrete, measures about 189 meters long and 156 meters wide, and could hold an estimated 50,000 spectators who entered through 80 numbered arches. It hosted gladiator fights, animal hunts, and public spectacles for nearly four centuries. Beneath the arena floor was a network of tunnels and cages with lifts that raised animals and scenery. Earthquakes and stone robbing over the centuries destroyed about two thirds of the original structure, but it remains one of Italy's most visited landmarks, attracting millions of tourists every year.
target_summary: Completed in 80 CE, Rome's Colosseum held about 50,000 spectators.

source: A typhoon is a powerful tropical cyclone that forms over warm ocean water in the western Pacific, where sea surface temperatures of at least 26.5 degrees Celsius provide the heat and moisture to fuel it. Warm, moist air rises, creating a low pressure area that draws in more air, which begins to spin because of Earth's rotation. The Philippines is hit by about 20 tropical cyclones every year. In November 2013, Typhoon Haiyan, known locally as Yolanda, struck the central Philippines with sustained winds of about 315 kilometers per hour and a storm surge that devastated Tacloban City, killing more than 6,000 people and displacing over four million.
target_summary: Typhoons form over warm seas; Haiyan killed over 6,000.

source: The French Revolution began in 1789, when widespread hunger, high taxes, and anger at the privileges of the nobility and clergy pushed the people of France to rebel against King Louis XVI. On July 14, 1789, a crowd stormed the Bastille, a royal prison in Paris that symbolized tyranny, and this date is still celebrated as France's national day. In August, the National Assembly adopted the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen, which proclaimed liberty and equality under the law. The monarchy was abolished in 1792, and Louis XVI was executed by guillotine in January 1793. The revolution ended in 1799 when Napoleon Bonaparte seized power.
target_summary: The 1789 storming of the Bastille began the French Revolution.

source: Republic Act 9003, the Ecological Solid Waste Management Act of 2000, requires Filipinos to separate their garbage at the source into biodegradable, recyclable, and residual waste. Every barangay is supposed to operate a Materials Recovery Facility where recyclables are sorted and kitchen scraps are turned into compost. The law also banned open dumps, but many remain in use today because cities lack money for sanitary landfills. In practice, enforcement is uneven: collection trucks often mix the segregated waste again, discouraging households from following the rules. Environmental groups say that the country needs stricter limits on single-use plastics, since the Philippines is one of the largest sources of plastic leaking into the ocean, with most of it flowing through rivers.
target_summary: Republic Act 9003 requires garbage segregation and barangay recovery facilities.

source: Siargao, a teardrop-shaped island in Surigao del Norte, is known as the Surfing Capital of the Philippines. Its most famous wave, Cloud 9, is a powerful reef break at General Luna that attracts surfers from around the world, and the town has hosted international surfing competitions since the 1990s. The best surf is usually between August and November, when swells arrive from the Pacific Ocean, although the waves are gentler in the dry months and suitable for beginners. Besides surfing, visitors can explore the Sugba Lagoon, the Magpupungko tidal pools, and the huge coconut palm forests along the Coconut Road. Siargao suffered heavy damage from Typhoon Odette in December 2021, but many resorts and cafes have been rebuilt.
target_summary: Siargao, the Philippines' surfing capital, is famed for Cloud 9.

source: English grammar traditionally recognizes eight parts of speech, which are categories of words based on their function in a sentence. Nouns name people, places, things, or ideas; pronouns replace nouns; verbs express actions or states; and adjectives describe nouns. Adverbs modify verbs, adjectives, or other adverbs, often telling how, when, or where something happens. Prepositions show relationships between words, such as in, on, or under, while conjunctions like and, but, and because join words or clauses. Finally, interjections express sudden emotions, as in wow or ouch. A single word can belong to different categories depending on its use: in the sentence she runs daily, run is a verb, but in the phrase a morning run, it is a noun.
target_summary: English grammar recognizes eight parts of speech, including nouns and verbs.

source: Isaac Newton published his three laws of motion in 1687 in a book titled Principia Mathematica. The first law, known as the law of inertia, states that an object at rest stays at rest and an object in motion keeps moving in a straight line at constant speed unless a force acts on it. The second law states that the force acting on an object equals its mass multiplied by its acceleration, written as F equals m times a, so a heavier object needs more force to speed up. The third law says that for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction, which explains why a rocket moves upward when it pushes hot gases downward. The same book also described the law of universal gravitation.
target_summary: Newton's 1687 laws cover inertia, force equals mass times acceleration, and reactions.

source: The Land Transportation Office announced that drivers caught using a mobile phone while driving will be fined PHP 5,000 starting next month, up from the current PHP 1,000 penalty. The new rule, which applies to texting, calling, and browsing, also adds a 15-day license suspension for repeat offenders. Agency data showed that distracted driving contributed to 17 percent of road crashes in Metro Manila last year, which killed 1,100 people. Traffic enforcers will use body cameras and fixed cameras at 60 intersections to catch violators. Drivers can still use phones for navigation if the device is mounted on the dashboard and used with hands-free voice commands. A three-week information campaign will run on radio and social media before enforcement begins.
target_summary: The LTO will raise the phone-while-driving fine to PHP 5,000 next month.

source: Electric vehicles run on electricity stored in large lithium-ion battery packs instead of burning gasoline or diesel, so they produce no exhaust from the tailpipe. An electric motor delivers instant power, making the cars quiet and quick to accelerate. Many models use regenerative braking, which turns the energy normally lost as heat during braking back into electricity to recharge the battery. A typical car can travel between 300 and 500 kilometers on a full charge. Charging at home with a standard outlet may take more than 10 hours, while a fast public charger can add 80 percent in about 30 minutes. The main obstacles are the high purchase price, limited charging stations, and the environmental cost of mining battery materials.
target_summary: Electric vehicles run on lithium-ion batteries and use regenerative braking.
